fields.definition: A humbucker wiring option that disconnects (typically shunts to ground) one of the pickup's two coils, leaving a single coil active. This produces a brighter, lower-output tone closer to a true single-coil, at the cost of the humbucker's hum cancellation.
fields.plain_english: A switch that shuts off one half of a two-coil (humbucker) pickup. With half turned off, the sound gets thinner and brighter, like a single-coil pickup.
fields.purpose_function: Gives one guitar two voices — full humbucker or brighter single-coil-like tone — from a single pickup, widening tonal range without swapping pickups.
fields.practical_application: A tech wires a push-pull pot or mini-toggle so activating it shunts one coil to ground; when tracking, the engineer selects the split setting for a cleaner, glassier rhythm tone.
common_mistakes: Confusing coil split with coil tap — splitting disables one whole coil of a humbucker, while tapping accesses a partial winding of a single coil.
Expecting a split humbucker to sound identical to a genuine single-coil; it is lower output and no longer hum-cancelling.
Forgetting to reconnect the coil-link/ground lead during the mod, leaving the pickup noisy or dead.
scenario_contexts: Wiring a push-pull tone pot on a Les Paul so each humbucker can be split for cleaner rhythm parts.
Recording a rhythm layer where a brighter, thinner tone cuts through a dense mix.
A player using split mode for clean/funk passages and full humbucker for lead.

sources: Seymour Duncan technical documentation — coil splitting/tapping

fields.definition: A pickup construction/wiring method in which an extra lead is connected to an intermediate point in a single coil's winding, allowing selection between the full number of turns (higher output, darker) and the tapped, partial winding (fewer turns, lower output, brighter). It is distinct from coil splitting, which disables one coil of a humbucker.
fields.plain_english: A pickup with an extra wire joined partway along its coil. It lets you switch between full power and a lower, brighter setting.
fields.purpose_function: Lets one pickup offer two output levels and voicings — a hotter modern sound and a lower-output vintage-like sound — from a single coil.
fields.practical_application: A tech connects the pickup's tap lead to a switch (often a push-pull pot); an engineer chooses the tapped setting for cleaner headroom or a brighter, vintage-flavoured track.
common_mistakes: Using 'coil tap' and 'coil split' interchangeably — they are electrically different.
Expecting a dramatic change; tapping mainly reduces output/turns, a subtler shift than splitting.
Assuming any pickup can be tapped — only pickups wound with a tap lead support it.
scenario_contexts: Selecting a tapped setting to reduce a hot pickup's output for a cleaner amp tone.
Wiring a switchable tap for two distinct output levels.
Blending a tapped, brighter tone into a layered rhythm track.

sources: Seymour Duncan technical documentation — coil tapping

fields.definition: A bowed-string playing technique in which the player uses the wooden stick of the bow on the strings instead of the hair. Two forms exist: col legno battuto (striking the string with the stick for a percussive, dry attack) and the rarer col legno tratto (drawing the wood across the string for a thin, glassy sustained sound).
fields.plain_english: Playing a string instrument with the wooden stick of the bow, not the hair. You tap or drag the wood on the strings. This gives a dry, clicky, spooky sound.
fields.purpose_function: Provides a distinctive percussive/colouristic string effect used for special orchestral and film-score textures.
fields.practical_application: When miking strings for a col legno passage, a technician uses a close mic to capture the quiet wood-on-string transient that a distant room mic would miss.
common_mistakes: Assuming col legno always means striking (battuto); tratto (drawn wood) is a separate, sustained variant.
Over-worrying bow damage — many players use a secondary bow, but light battuto on a normal bow is standard practice.
Under-miking the effect; its low level and sharp transient need close, careful gain staging.
scenario_contexts: Recording a horror or suspense film cue calling for eerie col legno strings.
A section playing col legno battuto for a rhythmic, percussive passage.
Close-miking a solo cello to catch the subtle wood-on-string attack.

sources: Samuel Adler, The Study of Orchestration

fields.definition: On an instrument with paired or grouped strings (a course), an unevenness between the strings of the same course in loudness, tuning, tone, or string age, so the pair no longer sounds as one unified note. It commonly appears on 12-string guitars, mandolins, and lutes.
fields.plain_english: On instruments where strings come in pairs, it is when the two strings of a pair do not match. One may be louder or slightly out of tune, so the pair sounds uneven.
fields.purpose_function: The term flags a specific fault so it can be diagnosed and corrected; a balanced course produces the rich, chorused sound that paired strings are meant to give.
fields.practical_application: A tech listens for beating or a weak string within each course and fixes it by tuning both strings precisely, matching string gauges, or replacing a dead string before tracking.
common_mistakes: Tuning only the main string of a course and ignoring its octave or unison partner
Blaming the room or mic for a beating, uneven sound that is really a course imbalance
Mixing a fresh string with a worn one in the same course, causing a tone and volume mismatch
scenario_contexts: Prepping a 12-string guitar before recording so each pair rings evenly
Diagnosing a beating, phasey chord on a mandolin during tracking
Checking octave-pair balance after changing one broken string

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians (course)
Baines, The Oxford Companion to Musical Instruments

fields.definition: A brass mute consisting of a straight-mute-like cone with an added cup that partly covers the bell of a trumpet, trombone, or similar instrument. It attenuates and rounds the tone, reducing upper harmonics to give a soft, muffled, mellow timbre darker than a straight mute.
fields.plain_english: A cup-shaped mute that fits over the bell of a trumpet or trombone to make it sound soft, muffled and mellow.
fields.purpose_function: Shapes brass timbre and lowers level for blended, subdued passages, common in jazz and big-band writing.
fields.practical_application: For a cup-muted horn, a technician may move the mic slightly off the bell axis and raise gain, since the mute both lowers output and darkens the tone.
common_mistakes: Confusing a cup mute with a straight mute; the cup adds a covering that darkens the sound further.
Miking a cup-muted horn as if it were open, then over-compensating for the lower, duller output.
Assuming all cup mutes are fixed — some have adjustable cups for varying the muffling.
scenario_contexts: Recording a big-band trumpet section written for cup mutes on a soft ballad.
A trombonist switching to cup mute for a mellow backing figure.
Setting mic gain for the reduced output of cup-muted brass.

sources: Samuel Adler, The Study of Orchestration

fields.definition: On a tonewheel (Hammond-type) organ, the set of sliding controls — typically nine per manual — that adjust the loudness of individual harmonic partials, labelled by organ-pipe footages (e.g., 16', 8', 4', 2 2/3'). Drawing bars out mixes these partials in an additive-synthesis fashion to build the instrument's timbre.
fields.plain_english: The sliders on a Hammond organ. Each one adds a different overtone to the sound. You mix them like faders to shape the tone you want.
fields.purpose_function: Give the player real-time additive control of tone colour by setting the balance of harmonics, from a pure flute-like tone to a full, bright registration.
fields.practical_application: When recording organ, an engineer notes the drawbar registration (e.g., 888000000) for recall and may re-voice the drawbars to fit the track rather than EQ heavily.
common_mistakes: Thinking drawbars are overall volume/EQ rather than level controls for individual harmonics.
Reading footage labels (16', 8', 4') as pure octaves while ignoring the 2 2/3' and 1 3/5' mutation ranks that add non-octave harmonics.
Failing to log drawbar settings, then being unable to reproduce a registration on overdub.
scenario_contexts: Dialing an 888000000 setting for a classic jazz organ tone.
Documenting a Hammond registration for later overdubs.
Adjusting drawbars instead of channel EQ to change organ brightness at the source.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments

fields.definition: A guitar or bass tuning in which one or more strings are lowered below standard pitch, most commonly the lowest string. In Drop D the 6th string is lowered a whole tone from E to D, giving a low root and one-finger power chords on the bottom three strings; deeper variants (Drop C, Drop B) transpose the whole set down and then drop the 6th.
fields.plain_english: Tuning a guitar's lowest string down to a lower pitch. Sometimes you drop all the strings. This gives a heavier, deeper sound and easy power chords.
fields.purpose_function: Extends the instrument's low range and simplifies power-chord fingering, central to hard rock and metal styles.
fields.practical_application: A tech sets up a guitar for drop tuning with heavier-gauge strings plus truss-rod and intonation adjustment so the slackened strings stay stable and in tune.
common_mistakes: Dropping to low tunings on light strings, causing floppy tension, poor intonation and fret buzz.
Skipping re-intonation and setup after a large tuning change.
Confusing Drop D (only the 6th string lowered) with a full-step-down tuning (all strings lowered).
scenario_contexts: Setting up a metal player's guitar in Drop C with heavier strings.
Retuning to Drop D for a single song's low riff.
Tracking a heavy rhythm part built on drop-tuned power chords.

fields.definition: In accordion and related free-reed instruments, a tuning in which the multiple reeds sounding a given note are set in strict unison (and octaves) with no deliberate offset, producing a clean tone with little or no tremolo beating. It contrasts with wet (musette) tuning, where reeds are intentionally detuned to create a beating, shimmering tremolo.
fields.plain_english: An accordion setup where each pair of reeds is tuned to the exact same pitch. The sound comes out clean and steady, with no wobble.
fields.purpose_function: Gives a straight, focused tone favoured in jazz, classical and some folk styles, avoiding the wavering tremolo of wet tuning.
fields.practical_application: When recording a dry-tuned accordion, an engineer captures a stable, non-warbling tone that sits cleanly in a mix without the chorus-like movement of a wet instrument.
common_mistakes: Assuming every accordion has the wavery 'musette' sound; dry-tuned instruments are deliberately beat-free.
Confusing dry/wet reed tuning with added studio effects such as chorus or detune.
Trying to 'fix' the tremolo with EQ — it is built into the reed tuning, not the frequency balance.
scenario_contexts: Recording a jazz accordionist who prefers a clean, dry-tuned tone.
Choosing a dry-tuned instrument to blend with a tightly tuned ensemble.
A tuner setting reeds in unison for a dry registration.

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (free-reed instruments)
flags: Topic mismatch: term is filed under Strings & Guitar but its established sense is an accordion/free-reed reed-tuning term; defined in that canonical sense per brief rule 6. Cross-confirmation limited — the underlying acoustics (unison vs. offset reed tuning and resulting tremolo/beating) is covered in free-reed acoustics literature, but acceptable sources using the specific trade label 'dry tuning' were scarce, hence Medium confidence.

fields.definition: A violin that produces its output primarily through electronic pickups (commonly piezoelectric transducers at the bridge, or magnetic systems) rather than an acoustic resonating body. Many are solid-body with minimal acoustic output, requiring amplification; some add extra strings (5-, 6-, or 7-string) to extend the range downward.
fields.plain_english: A violin that is quiet on its own. A pickup turns its shaking into a signal, which you send to an amp. Think of it as the electric-guitar version of a violin.
fields.purpose_function: Allows loud amplified performance without acoustic feedback and easy connection to effects, mixers and recording gear.
fields.practical_application: A technician takes the electric violin's output through a preamp/DI into a console or interface, and often adds reverb or effects since the raw solid-body signal is dry and direct.
common_mistakes: Plugging a high-impedance piezo output straight into a low-impedance mic/line input, loading the pickup and thinning the tone — use a proper high-impedance preamp/DI.
Expecting an acoustic violin tone from a bare solid-body signal, which is dry and needs reverb/EQ.
Assuming electric (solid-body) and electro-acoustic (acoustic with a fitted pickup) violins are the same thing.
scenario_contexts: DI'ing a solid-body electric violin into an interface for a pop session.
Amplifying a violinist on a loud stage without acoustic feedback.
Adding effects to an electric violin for a film or electronic production.

sources: Yamaha electric/silent violin technical documentation (SV series)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (instrument pickups and direct boxes)
